objection: Could the Bible have been changed to make Jesus divine?
answer:
The objection deserves a real answer rather than a dismissal, so let me take its two claims separately.

First, the textual point. If "God-language" for Jesus were a second-century insertion, we'd expect it to show up late in the manuscript stream and be absent from the earliest copies. The opposite is true: P52 (c. AD 125) already carries John's Gospel, and P66/P75 (c. 200) already contain "the Word was God" (John 1:1), "only-begotten God" (John 1:18), and Thomas's "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28) — all more than a century before Nicaea, with no evidence of an earlier, lower-Christology version being edited upward. Where real textual variants exist, like 1 Timothy 3:16 or Acts 20:28, the deity of Christ survives on either reading; scribal uncertainty never runs the direction the objection needs.

Second, the chronology. It's true Paul doesn't write "Jesus is theos" as a bare equation — but Paul is not our earliest layer; he quotes material older than himself. Philippians 2:6-11 is widely judged a pre-Pauline hymn, already applying to Jesus the words YHWH speaks of himself in Isaiah 45:23, within a few years of the crucifixion, among Jewish believers who reserved that language jealously for God alone. That is not late Greco-Roman deification-mythology drifting into a Jewish movement; it's Jewish monotheists including Jesus in the identity of the one God from the very start — worshiping him, praying to him, invoking his name in baptism, essentially at the beginning. John's Gospel doesn't introduce a new belief; it writes down, in fuller theological language, a confession Paul's letters presuppose and quote as already ancient.

So the doctrine didn't shape the text over decades of editing — the text we possess, at its earliest recoverable layer, already assumes the doctrine. That's a real difficulty for any theory of gradual invention, and it's worth naming plainly: the "late high Christology" model is not what the manuscripts or the pre-Pauline hymns actually show.

# Objection: The Divine Jesus Is a Later Addition to Scripture

Here's my concern: the passages that most clearly say Jesus *is* God — like John 1:1 or Thomas calling him "my God" in John 20:28 — appear mainly in the latest Gospel, written perhaps 90–100 AD when Greco-Roman ideas of divine men were circulating. The earlier epistles of Paul never once say "Jesus is God"; he consistently reserves "God" (*theos*) for the Father alone, calling Jesus "Lord" (*kyrios*). How confident can we be that later scribes and editors didn't insert or rewrite passages to elevate Jesus after the church had already decided, in the second century, that he must be divine? Couldn't the doctrine have shaped the text, rather than the text establishing the doctrine?

The objection deserves a real answer rather than a dismissal, so let me take its two claims separately.

First, the textual point. If "God-language" for Jesus were a second-century insertion, we'd expect it to show up late in the manuscript stream and be absent from the earliest copies.
